questions.stem: Which of the following is logically equivalent to (p ∧ q) → r?
questions.solution: The given statement can be rewritten using the definition of implication: (p ∧ q) → r is equivalent to ¬(p ∧ q) ∨ r. Therefore, option D is correct.
questions.explanation: This question tests understanding of proving logical equivalences by manipulating conditional statements and using De Morgan's laws.
questions.common_mistake_notes: A common mistake would be selecting C, which represents the converse of the original statement but not logically equivalent.

questions.stem: Which of the following is logically equivalent to ¬(p ∧ q) ↔ (¬p ∨ ¬q)?
questions.solution: The given statement is a biconditional, which can be rewritten as two implications: ¬(p ∧ q) → (¬p ∨ ¬q) and (¬p ∨ ¬q) → ¬(p ∧ q). These are equivalent to p → q and q → p, respectively. Therefore, option A is correct.
questions.explanation: This question assesses the ability to prove logical equivalences by understanding biconditionals and converting them into implications.
questions.common_mistake_notes: A common mistake would be selecting B, which represents material equivalence but does not capture the relationship between p and q in the original statement.

questions.stem: Which of the following is logically equivalent to (p → q) ∧ (q → r)?
questions.solution: The given statement can be simplified by applying the definition of implication: (p → q) ∧ (q → r) is equivalent to ¬p ∨ q and ¬q ∨ r. By using associativity, we get ¬p ∨ (q ∧ ¬q) ∨ r, which simplifies to ¬p ∨ r. This is equivalent to p → r. Therefore, option B is correct.
questions.explanation: This question tests understanding of manipulating compound statements and applying logical rules such as conjunction and disjunction.
questions.common_mistake_notes: A common mistake would be selecting A, which represents the converse relationship but not the same implication as the original statement.

questions.stem: Which of the following is logically equivalent to (p ∨ q) ↔ (¬p → q)?
questions.solution: The given statement can be rewritten as: (p ∨ q) ↔ ¬(¬p ∨ q). Using De Morgan's laws, this becomes: (p ∨ q) ↔ (p ∧ ¬q). By the distributive law, we get: p ∧ (q ∨ ¬q), which simplifies to p. Therefore, option D is correct.
questions.explanation: This question assesses the ability to prove logical equivalences by applying De Morgan's laws and understanding the relationship between disjunction and negation.
questions.common_mistake_notes: A common mistake would be selecting A, which represents a biconditional that does not hold for all values of p and q.

questions.stem: Which of the following is logically equivalent to (p ∧ q) ∨ (¬p ∧ r)?
questions.solution: The given statement can be simplified by using the distributive law: (p ∧ q) ∨ (¬p ∧ r) is equivalent to p ∧ (q ∨ ¬p) ∨ r. Since q ∨ ¬p is a tautology, it simplifies to p ∨ r. Therefore, option A is correct.
questions.explanation: This question tests understanding of manipulating compound statements and applying distributive law.
questions.common_mistake_notes: A common mistake would be selecting B, which represents only one possible case but not the complete logical equivalence.

questions.stem: Which of the following is logically equivalent to (p → q) ∨ (q → p)?
questions.solution: The given statement can be rewritten as: ¬p ∨ q and ¬q ∨ p. By using associativity, we get: (¬p ∨ q) ∧ (¬q ∨ p), which is equivalent to (p ∨ q) ∧ (¬p ∨ ¬q). Using De Morgan's laws, this becomes: (p ∨ q) ∧ ¬(p ∧ q). Since p ∨ q is a tautology, the entire expression simplifies to p ∨ q. Therefore, option C is correct.
questions.explanation: This question assesses the ability to prove logical equivalences by manipulating compound statements and applying De Morgan's laws.
questions.common_mistake_notes: A common mistake would be selecting A, which represents material equivalence but does not capture the relationship between p and q in the original statement.

questions.stem: Which of the following is logically equivalent to ¬(p ∧ q) ∨ (p ∧ ¬q)?
questions.solution: The given statement can be simplified by using De Morgan's laws: ¬(p ∧ q) ∨ (p ∧ ¬q) is equivalent to (¬p ∨ ¬q) ∨ (p ∧ ¬q). By the associative law, we get: ((¬p ∨ p) ∧ ¬q), which simplifies to ¬q. Therefore, option C is correct.
questions.explanation: This question tests understanding of manipulating compound statements and applying De Morgan's laws.
